doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Letting students stumble versus ready-made lessons
summary: Schools hand students everything; Jordan thinks stumbling leads to new ideas, and imitation of Brecker or Coltrane is not arrival.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: And if they stumble over it for a while, and sometimes if you let them stumble, now this is the part of jazz, this might be an important statement, this is the part of jazz that I think isn’t happening. They won’t let them try enough now, the schools are too lazy ‘cause they can go to the teachers and get jazz lessons and learn everything else, learn everything, the solo and all the technical aspects, all the embouchures, all the breathing, everything else is off. And they’re going to continue to do that, where if they stumble a while maybe some of them will stumble into a whole ‘nother thing. And maybe one of them kids we had today, their rhythm might be messed up and they’ll come out with another kind of rhythm to do something, their hearing will bring them somewhere, but if they’ve got everything written down for them and they’re playing it then, you know. Like the average kid now, a cat will say, “man I hear some kids say I’d love to play like Michael Brecker if I could” so and so and so. But they don’t know Michael Brecker’s got the technique to do that. He studied with some good people. And when they get to

Michael Brecker they say, “well man, I’ve arrived now.” I say all right, just remember you got Michael Brecker then. Just remember you got Coltrane. Just remember you got Charlie Parker when you get to that point. Your imitation of what they did. So that’s the thing.
